newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Uniform emission reduction approach flawed - ABARE.
newsitem.headline: Uniform emission reduction approach flawed - ABARE.

text.p: Countries must look beyond simplistic and unfair emission abatement approaches if the foundations of sound, long-term climate change policies are to be laid in Kyoto in December, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said in a statement.

Releasing ABARE's latest research report, The Economic Impact of International Climate Change Policy, acting deputy director Vivek Tulpule said uniform emission reduction targets proposed by some parties would impose significant economic costs on developed countries.

The uniform emission reduction approach did not take into account each country's individual economic and trade circumstances, with economic costs of emission abatement distributed unevenly between abating countries, he said.
ABARE estimates that the per-person economic costs imposed on Australia and Japan would be significantly higher than those imposed on the European Union and the United States, he said.
The adoption of a uniform emission abatement strategy would have negative consequences for key Australian export industries, he said.

Not only would Australia's coal exports decline relative to business-as-usual levels, but aluminium and iron and steel exports would suffer as Australian producers lost competitiveness relative to producers in developing countries such as South Korea and China, he said.

"The uneven distribution of economic costs does not lay the foundation for a wholehearted commitment to a climate change agreement, or an agreement that developing countries are likely to sign on to in the future," Tulpule said.
Developing countries were not required to reduce emissions under the Berlin Mandate and were projected to become the dominant global carbon dixoide emitters over the next couple of decades, he said.
Tradeable emission quotas had the potential to lower the total economic costs of emission abatement to the international community, he said.
Australia, formerly a strong proponent of international greenhouse emission controls, has tended to backtrack in recent years.

The conservative Liberal-National government said earlier this year that it would oppose any international deal for mandatory limits on such emissions because they would be contrary to the interests of Australia, a big coal exporter.
ABARE analysis showed that an appropriate initial allocation of quotas could be used to address inequitable outcomes from climate change action.
This provided a mechanism for reducing emissions that could encourage the participation of developing countries in the international emission abatement process, Tulpule said.

Industrialised nations have said they will push for an accord on quantified legally-binding objectives for emission limitations to be finalised at a climate change conference in Kyoto, Japan. The limitations would include significant emission reductions, they said.
